name: The Temple household
head: temple_john_t

arrival.note: 'Arrived early in July, 1833' (Andreas); the Baptist history transcription independently puts him at Chicago 'about 4 July 1833'. Recorded at not_later_than precision on the second source's date, because 'early in July' is a week and not a day. THE COMPILER'S SEASON SITS JUST OUTSIDE THIS BOUND AND DOES NOT MOVE IT. Moses and Kirkland vol. 1, printed page 90 (claim bk_mose1_005), names Dr. John T. Temple among the arrivals of the spring of 1833; this field is not_later_than 4 July 1833, on Andreas's "Arrived early in July, 1833" and the Baptist history's "about 4 July 1833" agreeing independently. Spring ends before either. TWO INDEPENDENT READINGS AT A WEEK'S PRECISION OUTWEIGH ONE SEASONAL LIST AT SIXTY YEARS' REMOVE, and the difference is small enough to be the compiler rounding a July arrival into the season of the men he lists it with. Recorded, not adopted. THE GRADE CEILING IS THE SOURCE'S AND NOT THIS FIELD'S. Moses and Kirkland, History of Chicago, Illinois (1895) is a compiler sixty years after the fact; every claim taken off it is transcription_mediated and none is scan_verified, so nothing drawn from it is graded above `inferred` (the rule T-1322 set for the settlers table, kept here).

arrival_year.note: A STATED YEAR, WHERE THE FIELD HELD A DRAW. The completed resident-research pass on temple_john_t read a municipal preservation study as corroborating Temple's July 1833 arrival with wife and four children, and his mail contract. The drawn year read 1833 too, so the value does not move; what moves is that it is now sourced. The same study gives dwelling and office locations that CONFLICT with this household's, and no address is taken from it here — the conflict is left standing where the pass recorded it. Under the evidence ladder ratified 2026-09-03 a source earlier than 1 July 1835 corroborates and dates and never promotes: the person's grade does not move on this.

party_size_on_arrival.note: Himself, a wife and four children - the source counts the party in terms. This is the only documented party size in the parcel.

origin.note: 'Came to Chicago from Washington, D. C.' - a from, not a birthplace.

reason_for_coming.value: A federal mail contract, Chicago to Fort Howard at Green Bay
reason_for_coming.note: 'Armed with a contract to carry the mails from Chicago to Fort Howard, Green Bay. His contract gave him a surety of a living, so that his surplus energy could well be used in the services of the Lord.' A man who came for a contract and built the town's first purpose-built place of worship and schooling with the proceeds.

lives_at.note: NOT ATTESTED, AND ONE NEAR MISS WORTH RECORDING. Peter Temple's advertisement of July 1834 puts 'the dwelling of Dr. J. T. Temple' on Franklin Street near Lake. This dataset holds no structure at that address, and the Temple Building at Franklin and South Water is a different building on the same street - a meeting house and school, not a residence. Linking the two would be wrong by a block and by a use.

works_at.note: He built it, headed its subscription with $100, and rented it out to whatever societies could pay. That is a proprietor's relation to a building rather than a workplace, and his medical practice and his stage line were carried on elsewhere. Linked because it is the building this town knew him by; graded derived because 'works at' overstates it.

present_on_scene_date.note: Continuously in the Chicago record 1833-1837 - stage line, Rush Medical College trustee in 1837, Board of Health in June 1835. Andreas's 'A Dr. Temple is stated by Colbert to have been appointed on the first permanent Board of Health in Chicago June 19, 1835' carries a footnote identifying him as John T. Temple, which is three weeks before the scene date.

persons.name: Dr John Taylor Temple

associated_with.note: GROUND HE BOUGHT, WHICH IS NOT GROUND HE STOOD ON — the rung is `tract` for that reason, and `land_purchased` is in neither the home kinds nor the work kinds because a holding is not a place a man was. The federal tract-sale register carries 8 row(s) — ls0353, ls0354, ls0355, ls0356, ls0357, ls0358, ls0359, ls0360 — to this purchaser, read as 'TEMPLE JOHN T', sorted onto school_section by tools/sort_land_sales_onto_tracts.py and covering about 21.1 acre(s) of it. THE TIER IS INFERRED AND THE TWO HALVES DIFFER: the purchase is documented — the register is a public record and states it — while the tie between that purchaser and THIS card is an identity ruling, upheld under T-0990 on 2026-09-11 by the rule 'TEMPLE JOHN T matches Dr John Taylor Temple: the forename names Dr John Taylor Temple of the 3 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full.'. The weaker half sets the tier. `to` is null because the register records a sale and not a tenure.

occupation.note: One of the eight physicians Andreas counts in the town at the close of 1833; he graduated at Middlebury College, Castleton, Vt., on 29 December 1830, and performed the first autopsy made in Chicago. Andreas adds that he 'is more intimately identified with these early days by reason of his stage line than of his medical practice' - he held the contract to carry the mail to Ottawa and made the first trip on 1 January 1834 with John Dean Caton as a passenger.

persons.note: THE BEST-DOCUMENTED ARRIVAL IN THE WHOLE PARCEL, and the only one that gives a month, a party size, an origin AND a reason in a single sentence. Andreas, scan p. 281: 'Dr. John T. Temple, who had arrived early in July, 1833, with his family, consisting of a wife and four children. He was a pious and earnest Baptist Christian, and came to Chicago from Washington, D. C., armed with a contract to carry the mails from Chicago to Fort Howard, Green Bay.' He then headed the subscription for the Temple Building with $100. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE.
